marrow__PHYS_CH14_Q001.takeaway: A spindle is built around 3–12 intrafusal muscle fibers.
marrow__PHYS_CH14_Q001.displayText: A muscle spindle contains about 3–12 intrafusal fibers arranged inside a capsule and in parallel with the larger extrafusal muscle fibers. The central region of each intrafusal fiber has few or no actin and myosin filaments and serves as the sensory region; contractile ends are driven by gamma motor fibers. The spindle is approximately 3–10 mm long; its central sensory region has few or no actin and myosin filaments, while the contractile ends receive small gamma motor fibers.

rationales.a: Twelve to twenty-four exceeds the stated spindle composition; the source gives 3–12 intrafusal fibers.
rationales.c: One to three is too few for the total intrafusal fibers in a spindle; that range describes nuclear bag fibers in the note.
rationales.d: Twenty-four to fifty is far above the source’s number of intrafusal fibers per spindle.

marrow__PHYS_CH14_Q002.takeaway: Gamma motor neurons innervate the muscle spindle.
marrow__PHYS_CH14_Q002.displayText: Gamma (γ) efferents provide motor supply to intrafusal fibers of the muscle spindle. Alpha motor neurons innervate the force-producing extrafusal fibers; spindle afferents instead carry sensory information from the receptor. The source gives gamma efferents as small group A motor fibers (about 3–6 μm), and notes approximately 1–3 nuclear bag and 3–9 nuclear chain fibers per spindle.

rationales.a: Group I afferents are sensory fibers, not the motor supply to spindle contractile ends.
rationales.b: Group II fibers provide secondary spindle sensory input; they are not the spindle’s motor efferents.
rationales.d: The spindle has dedicated gamma motor innervation; it is not without motor supply.

marrow__PHYS_CH14_Q003.takeaway: The yellow spindle-ending efferent is a gamma motor neuron.
marrow__PHYS_CH14_Q003.displayText: The yellow efferent fiber shown ending on the contractile portions of intrafusal fibers is a gamma motor neuron. Gamma motor neurons arise in the anterior horn and adjust spindle sensitivity and muscle tone. Alpha neurons innervate extrafusal fibers; beta and delta are not the labeled spindle efferent class. Gamma efferents average about 5 μm and supply intrafusal spindle fibers; alpha motor axons are larger (about 14 μm) and innervate extrafusal fibers. A-beta fibers carry touch/pressure and A-delta fibers pain/temperature.

rationales.b: Alpha motor neurons supply extrafusal force-producing fibers, not the spindle endings shown in yellow.
rationales.c: Beta is not the source-identified spindle efferent in the diagram; the spindle motor fibers are gamma efferents.
rationales.d: Delta is not the gamma efferent class that terminates on intrafusal spindle ends.

marrow__PHYS_CH14_Q005.displayText: Nuclear bag fibers within the spindle encode dynamic changes in muscle length. Nuclear bag fibers have nuclei in a central dilation and encode static plus dynamic length change; chain-fiber nuclei lie in rows and encode static length change.

rationales.d: The nuclear bag fibers have a defined sensory role: encoding dynamic muscle length.

marrow__PHYS_CH14_Q006.takeaway: Stretch-reflex afferents innervate nuclear bag and chain fibers.
marrow__PHYS_CH14_Q006.displayText: Deep tendon (stretch) reflexes use group Ia and group II spindle afferents. A primary Ia ending can contact dynamic bag, static bag, and nuclear chain fibers; group II secondary endings supply static bag and chain fibers. Golgi tendon organs use Ib afferents and detect tension, rather than serving as the spindle receptors for this reflex. Ia endings innervate dynamic bag, static bag, and chain fibers; group II endings innervate static bag and chain fibers. Both are involved in deep tendon/stretch reflexes.

rationales.a: Dynamic bag fibers are only one spindle class; Ia afferents also sample static bag and chain fibers, and group II supplies static bag/chain.
rationales.b: The Golgi tendon organ is a tension receptor with Ib afferents, not the receptor set for the deep tendon stretch reflex.
rationales.d: The tendon organ is not part of the spindle afferent pair asked for; the relevant endings are Ia and II on spindle fibers.

marrow__PHYS_CH14_Q007.takeaway: Passive muscle stretch activates the spindle and initiates the myotatic reflex.
marrow__PHYS_CH14_Q007.displayText: A stretch reflex is initiated by passive lengthening of the muscle, which stretches its muscle spindles and increases Ia afferent firing. The monosynaptic Ia-to-alpha motor-neuron connection contracts the stretched muscle; reciprocal inhibitory interneurons reduce antagonist activity. The monosynaptic myotatic arc proceeds from passive spindle stretch through Ia afferent activation to alpha motor-neuron drive and contraction of the same muscle.

rationales.b: Active shortening does not provide the passive muscle-lengthening trigger specified for the stretch reflex.
rationales.c: The question asks for the initiating stimulus, which is passive stretch rather than either passive or active movement indiscriminately.
rationales.d: A stretch reflex has a defined stimulus: passive stretch of the muscle spindle.

marrow__PHYS_CH14_Q008.takeaway: Withdrawal produces ipsilateral flexion and contralateral extension, not a symmetric bilateral response.
marrow__PHYS_CH14_Q008.displayText: The flexor-withdrawal response is a nociceptive polysynaptic reflex: ipsilateral flexors contract and extensors are inhibited to withdraw from the stimulus. A crossed-extensor response activates contralateral extensors and inhibits flexors to support balance. Thus the response is not the same on both sides. Pain afferents activate flexor reflexes polysynaptically; afterdischarge can hold the part away for about 0.1–3 seconds after irritation ends.

rationales.a: Nociceptive input is the usual trigger for the flexor-withdrawal reflex.
rationales.b: A sufficiently strong stimulus can maintain the polysynaptic withdrawal response through afterdischarge.
rationales.c: Ipsilateral flexion is the classic flexor-withdrawal pattern; it is not the false statement.

marrow__PHYS_CH14_Q009.takeaway: Intact reflex arcs are essential to normal postural maintenance.
marrow__PHYS_CH14_Q009.displayText: Normal posture depends on intact reflex arcs as well as descending control. Spinal reflexes and central pattern-generating circuits, together with brainstem and cerebellar postural systems, continuously adjust muscle activity against gravity. Muscle strength and joint range matter for movement but do not replace the reflex circuitry that stabilizes posture. Spinal cord circuits integrate reflexes and central pattern generators; brainstem and cerebellum govern postural reflexes; cortex and basal ganglia support voluntary movement.

rationales.b: Muscle strength helps generate movement, but posture also requires neural reflex control; power alone is not the defining dependency asked here.
rationales.c: Fiber type can influence contraction properties but does not substitute for the reflex arcs controlling posture.
rationales.d: A normal joint range permits movement, but posture maintenance depends on reflex and descending neural circuits.

marrow__PHYS_CH14_Q010.takeaway: The Golgi tendon organ is the receptor for the inverse stretch reflex.
marrow__PHYS_CH14_Q010.displayText: The Golgi tendon organ detects tension in series with muscle fibers. When tendon tension rises, Ib afferents activate an inhibitory interneuron that reduces alpha motor-neuron drive to the same muscle; this inverse stretch (Golgi tendon) reflex can relax the muscle. The spindle, by contrast, lies in parallel and detects muscle length. Golgi-organ Ib afferents recruit a glycinergic inhibitory interneuron that hyperpolarizes alpha motor neurons and relaxes the contracting muscle.

rationales.a: Muscle spindles lie in parallel and detect length/stretch; the inverse reflex uses tendon tension input.
rationales.b: Extrafusal fibers generate force but are not the sensory receptor for the inverse stretch reflex.
rationales.c: Intrafusal fibers belong to the spindle length receptor, not the tendon tension receptor.

marrow__PHYS_CH14_Q012.takeaway: The inverse stretch reflex has one interneuron between Ib afferent and motor output.
marrow__PHYS_CH14_Q012.displayText: The inverse stretch (Golgi tendon) reflex is disynaptic: Ib afferents from the Golgi tendon organ synapse on an inhibitory interneuron, which then inhibits the alpha motor neuron. Excessive tendon tension can produce rapid muscle relaxation, the lengthening reaction that protects muscle and tendon from overload. At extreme tendon tension, inhibition can cause near-immediate relaxation (the lengthening reaction), a protective response against muscle tearing or tendon avulsion.

rationales.a: Ia spindle afferents mediate the stretch reflex; inverse stretch begins with Ib tendon-organ afferents.
rationales.b: Although Golgi tendon input initiates it, this reflex includes an inhibitory interneuron and is not monosynaptic.
rationales.d: A single interneuron is inserted in this disynaptic circuit; it is not a long polysynaptic chain.

marrow__PHYS_CH14_Q013.takeaway: Withdrawal afferents reach motor neurons through spinal interneurons, not a direct pathway.
marrow__PHYS_CH14_Q013.displayText: The flexor-withdrawal pathway is polysynaptic. Nociceptive afferents first recruit spinal interneuron pools, which distribute excitation to the necessary flexors, inhibit antagonists, and sustain afterdischarge. They do not project directly to anterior motor neurons; the shortest described route uses several neurons. The source identifies diverging withdrawal circuits, reciprocal inhibition, and afterdischarge; the shortest pathway is three or four neurons.

rationales.a: Diverging interneuron circuits spread excitation to the muscle groups needed for withdrawal.
rationales.b: Reciprocal inhibition of antagonist muscles is part of the flexor-withdrawal circuit.
rationales.c: Interneuronal afterdischarge can prolong the reflex after the initiating stimulus ends.

marrow__PHYS_CH14_Q014.takeaway: Ongoing spindle input contributes to baseline muscle tone.
marrow__PHYS_CH14_Q014.displayText: Muscle spindle input helps maintain muscle tone, the resistance a muscle offers to passive stretch. Ongoing group Ia and II afferent activity supports baseline alpha motor-neuron firing through the tonic stretch-reflex circuit. The Golgi tendon organ instead senses tension; Renshaw cells mediate recurrent inhibition. The tonic/static stretch-reflex circuit uses ongoing Ia and II spindle afferent activity to support baseline alpha motor-neuron firing.

rationales.a: The Golgi tendon organ senses tension and can inhibit muscle output; it is not the principal source of baseline stretch-reflex tone.
rationales.c: Renshaw cells provide recurrent inhibition within spinal motor circuits, not the tonic length feedback that supports muscle tone.
rationales.d: Muscle tone has a defined spindle-mediated reflex contribution, so ‘none’ is incorrect.

marrow__PHYS_CH14_Q015.takeaway: Alpha and gamma motor neurons are coactivated to keep the spindle responsive during contraction.
marrow__PHYS_CH14_Q015.displayText: During many voluntary and involuntary movements, alpha and gamma motor neurons are coactivated. Alpha drive contracts extrafusal fibers while gamma drive contracts intrafusal ends, keeping the spindle’s sensory region taut as the whole muscle shortens. This preserves spindle feedback during movement. Alpha–gamma coactivation keeps the spindle receptor region from going slack or being overstretched as the whole muscle contracts, preserving length feedback for ongoing and planned movement.

rationales.a: Alpha activation alone would shorten the muscle and unload the spindle unless gamma drive also contracts intrafusal ends.
rationales.b: Gamma-before-alpha is not the described coordinated pattern; the two motor systems are excited at nearly the same time.
rationales.d: Alpha-only drive would let the spindle slacken during shortening and reduce useful length feedback.

marrow__PHYS_CH14_Q016.takeaway: Righting reflexes are postural reflexes that restore orientation.
marrow__PHYS_CH14_Q016.displayText: Righting reflexes are postural responses that restore normal orientation, including keeping the head upright and maintaining standing position. Much of this righting-reflex integration occurs in midbrain nuclei, linking vestibular and other sensory cues to corrective movement. These orienting responses are integrated mainly in midbrain nuclei and maintain upright head and standing posture.

rationales.a: A stretch reflex is a local muscle-length response, not the broader orienting response that rights the body.
rationales.c: Righting reactions are integrated above the spinal cord, prominently in the midbrain, rather than being purely spinal.
rationales.d: Visual/ocular reflexes can contribute sensory input, but the righting response is a postural reflex category.

marrow__PHYS_CH14_Q017.takeaway: The footpad supportive reaction is spinally integrated, so calling it a midbrain righting reflex is false.
marrow__PHYS_CH14_Q017.displayText: Pressure applied to the footpad of a decerebrate animal can trigger the positive supportive reaction: the limb extends toward the pressure. The response is also called the magnet reaction; it can occur after spinal transection and helps prevent falling toward that side. Its integration is spinal, not a midbrain righting reflex. The magnet reaction is observed in infants and after spinal transection; pressure on the right footpad, for example, extends the right lower limb.

rationales.a: The pressure-directed extension is called the magnet reaction, so this statement is true.
rationales.b: The supportive reaction can be integrated at spinal level, including after spinal transection.
rationales.c: Extending toward the applied pressure helps support the body and prevent falling on that side.

marrow__PHYS_CH14_Q018.takeaway: The medullary pyramids are formed by corticospinal fibers.
marrow__PHYS_CH14_Q018.displayText: The corticospinal pathways are called pyramidal tracts because their fibers form the visible pyramids on the ventral medulla. Vestibular, reticular, and rubrospinal pathways descend outside this medullary pyramid system and are classified as extrapyramidal. The corticospinal tract makes a triangular bundle along the ventral medulla, where it forms the visible pyramids.

rationales.a: The arcuate nucleus is a medullary structure but does not form the corticospinal pyramids.
rationales.b: Vestibular nuclei give rise to vestibulospinal pathways, which are extrapyramidal.
rationales.c: The interstitial nucleus of Cajal participates in gaze and postural control; it is not the tract forming the medullary pyramids.
